content.comment_body: Hello [user_name], [user_name], [user_name], and all experts, From what I know, the modular [product_name] can have a maximum of 24 digital inputs, 8 analog inputs, 16 digital outputs, and 2 analog outputs. However, my project requires more than 21 digital inputs and over 24 digital outputs. I'm new to PLC software and control systems. Could experts please share recommendations and advice on which [product_name] would suit my needs? Wishing everyone a Merry Christmas! Looking forward to your responses. Best regards, [user_name].
Hi [user_name], You could consider using [product_name] from the [version_no] series. These are suitable for small automation projects and offer more options than the [product_name] modules.

Hi, [user_name]. One option is to use two [product_name] modules. For example: [url] This logic module is easy to program and operate, letting you integrate it into various systems quickly. Alternatively, you might consider products like the [product_name] or [product_name] from the [version_no] series.

Where did I put those extra digital outputs? If you need up to 28 digital outputs, try this: 1) Use two [product_name] units; the second can be a [product_name] variant without a display for cost savings (even secondhand options are available). 2) On the main [product_name], use only 12 digital outputs directly in your program. 3) Connect the last 4 digital outputs from the first module to 4 digital inputs on the second module. 4) Implement combinational logic in the first module using basic functions to multiplex (using digital logic, not analog) up to 16 additional outputs into a 4-bit binary 'address.' 5) On the second module, create a simple logic program to translate those input bits into the required 16 digital outputs. 6) The switching speed will match the cycle time of the [product_name]. 7) Be cautious when all 4 inputs are off ('0000'), since this will still activate a particular output based on your logic arrangement. 8) Maybe I'll develop a sample program for this. Goodbye! Aaaaaarrrgghhh!

That's an idea. I'm not sure which outputs respond to which signals. With a maximum of 16 outputs, you'll have 8 remaining outputs (24-16 = 8). If some outputs are for system status indications (like control lamps), you could use a [product_name] operator device for display purposes.

Here's a multi-output solution—consider it a gift to everyone! By using two [product_name] units (each with full expansion modules) and connecting 4 wires from outputs on module 1 to inputs on module 2, it's possible to have a main program with up to 27 digital outputs. You'd have one additional spare digital output on module 2 for remote control needs. This approach is scalable; you can split your program across various modules, each handling different system sections, with simple data exchange between them. Enjoy experimenting with this!
